summary:
Soon the Moon could be the ultimate destination for all to explore. But where should we land, and when? A good landing day needs two things in the sky: the Sun, for power, and Earth in view, to communicate back home. Choosing where and when to land is one of the first decisions of every Moon mission, and Tanaw lets anyone experience it.

Tanaw is a lunar travel guide that shows where the Sun and Earth sit above a chosen site's horizon and gives a Go or No-go advisory. Pick a date that matters to you, and see the sky from where you would stand. On a No-go day, Tanaw suggests another date or another site. Compare two lunar landing sites side by side to find the best place and time to visit the Moon.
details:
What it does

Tanaw shows, for any landing site on the Moon and any date, whether the Sun and Earth are above the local horizon. It opens on the Moon with landing sites from past and planned missions and candidate regions near the south pole, and any other point can be picked on the globe. For the chosen site and date it gives a Go or No-go call, the hours of sunlight and of Earth in view, the next rise and set times, and a day-by-day forecast. The sky view draws the site's skyline with the Sun's path and Earth's small loop over it, so you can see what blocks them. Sites can be compared on the same dates, viewed in 3D, shown with sunlight, permanent-shadow and slope layers, and searched by stay length, sunlight hours, Earth visibility and terrain.

How it works

The Moon has no atmosphere, so the horizon is set by terrain and the Moon's curvature alone. We compute each site's skyline from NASA LOLA elevation data (polar maps at 240 m and 20 m per pixel, 5 m maps near south-pole sites, SLDEM2015 elsewhere). Sun and Earth positions as seen from each site come from NASA/JPL Horizons every 10 minutes and are checked against NASA NAIF SPICE. Python scripts compare the two and publish the results as static files, so the site needs no server and loads quickly. Dates outside the saved forecast year use a browser-side estimate, labelled as an estimate.

Benefits and intended impact

When a launch or hardware delay moves a landing, planners need to know which days and which nearby sites still work. Tanaw answers that on one screen instead of a series of queries in Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons, and the skyline shows why a day fails, which helps science and engineering teams agree on a trade-off. The same view lets students and the public see why the lunar south pole is so hard to plan for. We want a tool a planner can open during a schedule meeting and a student can open in class.

How it is creative

Tanaw treats the Moon like a place you are travelling to and checking the forecast for: a call for the day, a few numbers and a strip of days, in place of ephemeris tables. The sky view puts the terrain skyline, the Sun's path and Earth's loop in one picture, so the reason behind each call is visible. The name Tanaw is Filipino for looking into the distance, which is what the app does from each landing site.

Tools and languages

HTML, CSS and JavaScript with three.js for the globe and 3D views; TypeScript for the browser-side estimate; Python with NumPy, SpiceyPy and jsonschema for the precomputed science; automated browser checks with Playwright. Hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Source code under Apache 2.0: https://github.com/ruzcko/gabay-tanaw

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy over approximation: published forecasts come from real terrain and NASA/JPL ephemerides, and anything estimated is labelled as an estimate.
  • Terrain detail: higher-resolution elevation near south-pole sites, where small ridges decide whether the Sun is visible.
  • Earth's libration: Earth's small loop in the sky is part of the computed positions, so Earth visibility includes it.
  • Public understanding: no prior knowledge needed. A plain Go or No-go call, a few numbers and the skyline picture explain what an ephemeris table would not.
  • Fun, in anticipation of lunar travel: Tanaw treats a Moon landing like a trip you are planning. You search destinations the way you would on a booking site, by length of stay, sunlight and Earth in view, so exploring the Moon feels like planning a visit.
  • Open data and credit: every dataset, library and font is listed with its licence in SOURCES.md.

Team Gabay

We are a team from the Philippines bringing science, design, and curiosity together to make space exploration accessible. Our name, Gabay, means “guide” in Filipino, and we’re building one to help scientists and the public explore and compare lunar landing sites.

Ruzcko (Rogelio Ruzcko Tobias, @ruzcko) and Lance (Ferdinand Lance Bundoc, @fcbundoc).
